summary.text: Apollo 11 was the American mission of July 1969 that first landed humans on the Moon.
Armstrong and Aldrin went down to the surface and walked on it while Collins stayed in lunar orbit, and all three then returned safely and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean.
It met the goal Kennedy set in 1961, to land a man on the Moon and bring him back safely within the decade, at the height of the Space Race with the Soviet Union.

facts.label: Landing site
facts.value: The Sea of Tranquility, on July 20

items.prompt: The Soviets had more powerful launchers than the Americans. Why did that push Kennedy toward a Moon landing as the national goal?

options.label: The Soviets had promised to help build the American spacecraft
American launchers were stronger, so a win was certain
It was beyond existing launch vehicles, so both started level
A Moon landing was the cheapest project on the table

items.explain: Kennedy chose a challenge that exceeded what the existing generation of rockets could do, so neither country would have a head start.

items.prompt: Two of the three astronauts took the landing craft down to the surface. Where was the third?

options.label: Waiting on the surface beside the landing craft
Circling the Moon in the command module Columbia
Back on Earth, working at mission control
Riding down inside the descent stage of Eagle

items.explain: Collins stayed in lunar orbit aboard Columbia while Armstrong and Aldrin descended in Eagle.

items.prompt: In 1957 the Soviet Union put the first artificial satellite into space, alarming many Americans. How did the United States respond?

options.label: It created NASA and started a program to put a man in orbit
It dismissed the satellite as having no military meaning
It offered the Soviets a joint mission to the Moon at once
It landed astronauts on the Moon within the following year

items.explain: Sputnik showed the Soviets could threaten American claims of superiority, so Eisenhower created NASA and began Project Mercury.

items.prompt: By May 1961 an American, Alan Shepard, had flown in space, yet the Soviets were said to hold the lead. Why?

options.label: Shepard flew first, but his flight was cut short
Both men circled the Earth, but one made more laps
Neither had circled the Earth, but one stayed up longer
Gagarin went first and orbited; Shepard's 15 minutes did not

items.explain: Gagarin was the first person in space and the first to orbit the Earth, while Shepard's short flight, almost a month later, was suborbital.

items.prompt: Despite early leads in spaceflight, the Soviet Union did not land people on the Moon first. What was it unable to match?

options.label: The number of American satellites in orbit
The skill of the American pilots
The Saturn V rocket
The size of the American television audience

items.explain: The Soviet Union could not match the Saturn V rocket, and its uncrewed probe Luna 15 crashed on the Moon.

items.prompt: In June 1961 Kennedy suggested the two superpowers make the Moon landing a joint project. How did Khrushchev respond?

options.label: He accepted, and Soviet engineers joined NASA's work
He declined the proposal
He accepted, but the plan ended after Kennedy died
He answered with a plan for a Soviet-only landing

items.explain: Khrushchev turned the offer down, and the idea of a joint mission was later abandoned after Kennedy's death.

paragraphs.heading: The first Moon landing
paragraphs.text: Apollo 11 was the American mission, flown from July 16 to 24, 1969, that first put people on the Moon. It was the fifth flight with a crew in NASA's Apollo program. Neil Armstrong was the commander, Michael Collins flew the command module, and Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin flew the lunar module; for each man it was his second and last spaceflight.

paragraphs.heading: Why it was flown
paragraphs.text: Apollo 11 was the high point of the Space Race, a Cold War contest between the United States and the Soviet Union. In October 1957 the Soviets launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, and the shock set off the race. They took the lead again in April 1961, when Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space. Because Soviet rockets could lift more, President Kennedy picked a goal beyond any existing rocket, so both sides would start level: a crewed trip to the Moon. In May 1961 he challenged the country to land a man on the Moon and bring him home safely before the decade was out.

paragraphs.heading: Down to Tranquility
paragraphs.text: After three days of travel, Armstrong and Aldrin took the lunar module Eagle down to the Sea of Tranquility on July 20, while Collins stayed in orbit in the command module Columbia. About six hours after landing, Armstrong stepped out as the first human ever to walk on the Moon, and Aldrin followed him 19 minutes later. In roughly two and a half hours outside, they planted an American flag, talked with President Nixon at the White House, set up science instruments, and gathered 21.5 kg of lunar material.

paragraphs.heading: The world watched
paragraphs.text: Armstrong's walk was shown live on television to an estimated 600 million people, about a fifth of the world's population, making it one of the most-watched broadcasts ever. As he stepped down, he called it a small step for a man and a giant leap for mankind. The samples the crew brought home led scientists to three minerals no one had recognized before. The instruments left on the surface kept sending back data for years.

paragraphs.heading: Coming home
paragraphs.text: After more than 21 hours on the surface, Armstrong and Aldrin went back up to lunar orbit to rejoin Collins, and all three splashed down safely in the Pacific Ocean on July 24. Meanwhile the Soviet Union's uncrewed probe Luna 15 crashed into the Moon on July 21, while the two Americans were still on the surface. Back home the crew were honored with ticker-tape parades, a goodwill tour around the world, and the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Today the command module Columbia is preserved in Washington, D.C., at the National Air and Space Museum, and the descent stage of Eagle is still on the Moon.
